title: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
summary: Exfiltration over another network medium means moving collected data out of a target through a path that is not the primary command and control route, for example a wireless connection, a mobile data link, a modem line, a Bluetooth pairing or another radio channel. The technique exists because such paths often sit outside the defended enterprise network: they bypass web proxies, mail gateways and the firewall rules that guard the main internet connection, and they may not appear in the monitoring stack at all. The data is still gathered and staged first, so this behaviour normally appears together with collection, archiving and optional encryption. Evidence tends to be physical or host based rather than network based. Defenders look for hosts with unexpected wireless or cellular interfaces enabled, servers with radio hardware that has no business reason to be there, new pairings, and outbound volume that never appears in any proxy or firewall record.

beginner.definition: This technique means sending stolen data out of a building by a different route than the usual internet link. The normal route is the wired company network. The other route could be wireless, a mobile phone network, or a short range radio link. The attacker hopes this second route is watched less carefully.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security monitoring sits on the main network path. A second path may carry data straight past those checks. Data can leave through a phone in someone's pocket without touching the company firewall. If you never look at these paths, you may never see the theft at all.
howItWorks: The attacker collects files on the machine and packs them into one or more archives.
They check whether another network path is available, such as wireless or mobile data.
They connect the machine, or a nearby device, to that other path.
They send the packed data over it, often in small pieces over time.
The data arrives on infrastructure the attacker controls, away from the main network.
They may remove signs of the transfer, such as saved profiles or temporary files.
beginner.example: Think of an office where every visitor must sign in at the front desk. The guard watches that door all day. A thief who wants to remove a box of documents does not use the front door. They pass the box through a side window to a waiting car, or hand it to a rider at the back gate. Nothing is written in the visitor book. The main door stays guarded and useless, because the thief never went through it.
takeaways: Data can leave through paths that your main network monitoring never sees.
Servers and desktops rarely need wireless or radio hardware, so treat it as suspicious.
Physical and endpoint records matter as much as network logs for this technique.

objectives: Explain why an attacker would choose a medium other than the main command and control path.
List common alternate media such as wireless, cellular data, modem and radio links.
Describe the endpoint evidence these transfers leave behind.
Compare network based and host based detection options for this technique.
Recommend policy controls that limit unnecessary network interfaces on servers.
